title: Burst noise hypothesis lab notes
content:
Summary:
I ran a small lab to reproduce the late-night throughput dips we saw across the gamma and delta dedicated pools. This doc captures the timeline, experiments, quick remediation steps that worked (and those that didn't), and a minimal on-call cheat-sheet for next occurrence.

Goals:
- Reproduce burst / noisy-tenant signal locally on a staging cluster that mirrors a dedicated pool.
- Verify allocator behavior around fanout spikes and eviction thresholds.
- Test quick containment/mitigation knobs for oncall use.

High-level hypothesis (still tentative):
- The coupling of short-lived bursty tenants (lots of small inference requests with high KV cache churn) + allocator fanout leads to transient memory pressure inside the pod and driver-level slowdowns.
- Driver/firmware DVFS responses to thermal/telemetry changes amplify token latency, creating a throughput spiral.
- Autoscaler hysteresis + label fragmentation prevents fast re-scheduling to cold nodes, so degraded pods remain pinned and cause a noisy-neighbor effect.

Incident timeline (replay from staging hammer run):
- 2026-03-01 02:10 UTC - start synthetic hammer: 300 concurrent small-gen requests (seq len 32), repeating random prefixes.
- 2026-03-01 02:13 UTC - first per-pod p99 latency drift (25% over baseline). CPU on node stable, GPU sm utilization starts to oscillate.
- 2026-03-01 02:16 UTC - allocator registers high fanout events: many tiny containers created then destroyed (bursty job churn).
- 2026-03-01 02:17 UTC - KV cache misses spike; observed frequent cache flushes in runtime logs.
- 2026-03-01 02:20 UTC - kernel queue backlog grows, driver logs show queued submissions backlog (nvml/driver latency).
- 2026-03-01 02:22 UTC - autoscaler scale-up triggered but delayed due to label mismatch: new nodes not eligible for this pool because of affinity label fragmentation (old jobs left stale labels).
- 2026-03-01 02:25 UTC - partial mitigation: we forced eviction on oldest ephemeral sessions and disabled aggressive cache invalidation in runtime; throughput recovered slowly over 6 minutes.

What we learned (evidence):
- Allocator fanout is the earliest leading indicator (see allocator logs) — spikes predate p99 latency. Keeping an eye on "create/delete rate" for pods is a cheap signal.
- KV cache churn correlates with per-token CPU overhead and increased GPU kernel launches (more small kernels).
- Autoscaler label eligibility logic needs a guard: if labels are stale/fragmented, scale decisions are delayed.

Commands and queries used in the lab (copy/paste friendly):
- Watch pod create/delete rate: kubectl --context=staging get events --watch --field-selector involvedObject.kind=Pod | grep -E "Created|Deleted"
- Allocator tail (staging): kubectl -n allocator logs -l app=allocator -f | grep -E "fanout|create_pod|delete_pod"
- Check KV cache flush events in runtime logs: kubectl -n runtime logs <runtime-pod> | egrep "kv_cache|flush|invalidate"
- Driver queue backlog quick-check (node): sudo dmesg | tail -n 200 | egrep "nv|gpu|cu:"
- Metric: rate(allocator_pod_creates_total[1m]) and rate(allocator_pod_deletes_total[1m]) in Graphite/Prometheus

Quick on-call runbook (minimal, tested in lab):
1) Identify: confirm pod create/delete rate > 100/min for dedicated pool for 2 consecutive minutes AND p95 latency > baseline+20%. If both true, move to containment.
2) Contain: add temporary admission control by annotating pool config to reject new small-batch classes for 5 minutes: kubectl patch cm pool-config -n infra --type merge -p '{"data":{"reject_small_batches":"true"}}'
   - Notes: this reduces churn; we tested in staging and saw create/delete rate fall ~70% in 3m.
3) Fast route: scale ephemeral-burst pool up by +2 nodes to absorb bursts: ./scripts/scale-pool --pool ephemeral-burst --delta 2
4) If node label fragmentation prevents autoscaler, run label reconciliation: ./bin/label-reconcile --pool <pool> --fix-stale-labels
5) If driver backlog persists > 10m, escalate to infra-driver with logs: /var/log/nvidia/driver.log (attach last 500 lines). Consider rolling reboot of affected nodes (careful: kicks existing workloads).

What worked in staging:
- Temporary admission control (reject_small_batches) + scale ephemeral pool recovered p95 in ~4-6 min.
- Label reconciliation prevented autoscaler stalls and allowed scale-out when retried.

What didn't help / false leads:
- Increasing eviction aggressiveness (early experiment) made things worse by causing more churn.
- Cross-pool fallback to hosted-tier introduced high latency and customer-visible errors in our sim (not acceptable).

Instrumentation additions (todo):
- Add allocator fanout rate metric as an alertable signal (SRE): allocator_pod_fanout_rate with threshold > 50/min.
- Track per-pod KV cache flush rate and expose percentiles (p50/p95).
- Add autoscaler label-mismatch counter metric when node pool rejected scale (helps detect fragmentation).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Is driver DVFS/thermal telemetry actually gating kernel throughput, or are we misattributing (i.e., is the driver backlog purely a submission burst)? Need to coordinate with hardware/driver team to add telemetry correlation.
- Why did cache invalidation ramp up so quickly at the start of bursts? Is this consumer behavior (prompts) or runtime bug?
- Long-term: would a small request-size classification at the API gateway (reject or batch tiny requests) provide better control than admission control at pool config? Pros/cons: gateway rule is lower latency but more invasive.

Follow-ups assigned:
- Marcus Li: add allocator fanout metric + alert (due 2026-03-15).
- Priya Nambiar: prototype gateway small-batch classifier and run A/B in staging (due 2026-03-22).
- Ava Chen (me): schedule driver telemetry sync with HW/driver team to validate DVFS hypothesis (meeting by 2026-03-12).

Retrospective notes (short):
- Root cause is multi-factor: short-lived bursty tenants create high create/delete rates -> allocator fanout -> KV cache churn -> driver submission backlog -> autoscaler delays due to label fragmentation -> cascade. No single component failure.
- Mitigation strategy should focus on early detection (fanout alert) + fast containment (admission control + ephemeral absorb), and long-term on better admission control at the API edge + resiliency in autoscaler label handling.

Notes to self (casual):
- Save this exact hammer script in /scripts/hammers/burst_noise_0326.sh with env toggles for seq-len and concurrency.
- When running oncall drills, force label fragmentation scenario to make sure runbook actually helps.

Appendix: snippets from logs (redacted):
[allocator] 02:16:10 fanout=78 creates=62 deletes=59 pool=gamma
[runtime] 02:17:03 kv_cache flush keys=423 miss_rate=0.72 pod=runtime-az2
[driver] 02:20:40 submission_delay_ms avg=72 p95=430 node=node-14

If you read nothing else: focus on allocator fanout and add a simple admission control knob that the oncall can flip in < 2 minutes.

-- Ava
